name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q01 - Ground state electronic configurations of 3d elements

questiontext.text:
Match the \(3d\)-series elements in List I with their ground-state outer electronic configurations in List II:

List I (Element)List II (Outer Configuration)
(1) \(\mathrm{Sc}\) (\(Z=21\))(A) \(3d^{10}4s^2\)
(2) \(\mathrm{Cr}\) (\(Z=24\))(B) \(3d^1 4s^2\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Cu}\) (\(Z=29\))(C) \(3d^5 4s^1\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Zn}\) (\(Z=30\))(D) \(3d^{10}4s^1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the \(3d\) transition series, electrons generally fill the \(4s\) orbital first and then the \(3d\) orbitals, except where half-filled (\(3d^5\)) or completely filled (\(3d^{10}\)) configurations provide extra stability.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Scandium (\(Z=21\)) has 3 valence electrons outside the \([\mathrm{Ar}]\) core, giving \(3d^1 4s^2\). Chromium (\(Z=24\)) adopts \(3d^5 4s^1\) instead of \(3d^4 4s^2\) due to the stability of the half-filled \(3d\) subshell. Copper (\(Z=29\)) adopts \(3d^{10}4s^1\) instead of \(3d^9 4s^2\) due to the stability of the completely filled \(3d\) subshell. Zinc (\(Z=30\)) has 12 valence electrons outside \([\mathrm{Ar}]\), giving \(3d^{10}4s^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{Sc} \rightarrow 3d^1 4s^2\), \(\mathrm{Cr} \rightarrow 3d^5 4s^1\), \(\mathrm{Cu} \rightarrow 3d^{10}4s^1\), and \(\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow 3d^{10}4s^2\), corresponding to (1)-(B), (2)-(C), (3)-(D), (4)-(A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q02 - Transition metal catalysts and industrial processes

questiontext.text:
Match the catalysts in List I with the corresponding industrial processes in List II:

List I (Catalyst)List II (Process)
(1) \(\mathrm{V}_2\mathrm{O}_5\)(A) Manufacture of polythene (Ziegler catalyst)
(2) Finely divided \(\mathrm{Fe}\)(B) Oxidation of ethyne to ethanal (Wacker process)
(3) \(\mathrm{TiCl}_4 + \mathrm{Al(CH}_3)_3\)(C) Oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) in Contact Process
(4) \(\mathrm{PdCl}_2\)(D) Manufacture of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) in Haber process

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition metals and their compounds act as effective catalysts due to their ability to adopt multiple oxidation states and form complexes or surface intermediates.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Vanadium(V) oxide (\(\mathrm{V}_2\mathrm{O}_5\)) catalyses the oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) to \(\mathrm{SO}_3\) in the Contact Process for sulphuric acid. Finely divided iron catalyses ammonia synthesis from \(\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) in the Haber process. \(\mathrm{TiCl}_4\) with \(\mathrm{Al(CH}_3)_3\) forms the Ziegler catalyst for manufacturing polyethylene (polythene). \(\mathrm{PdCl}_2\) catalyses the oxidation of ethyne to ethanal in the Wacker process.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are (1)-(C), (2)-(D), (3)-(A), (4)-(B).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q03 - Colours of aquated 3d transition metal ions

questiontext.text:
Match the aquated \(3d\)-series ions in List I with their characteristic colours in aqueous solution in List II:

List I (Aquated Ion)List II (Colour)
(1) \(\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}\) (\(3d^0\))(A) Pink
(2) \(\mathrm{Ti}^{3+}\) (\(3d^1\))(B) Blue
(3) \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) (\(3d^5\))(C) Colourless
(4) \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) (\(3d^9\))(D) Purple

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The colour of aquated transition metal ions arises from \(d\text{–}d\) electronic transitions when an electron is excited from a lower-energy \(d\) orbital to a higher-energy \(d\) orbital by absorbing visible light.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
\(\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}\) has a \(3d^0\) configuration with no \(d\) electrons for \(d\text{–}d\) transition, so it is colourless. \(\mathrm{Ti}^{3+}\) (\(3d^1\)) is purple in aqueous solution. \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) (\(3d^5\)) is pale pink. \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) (\(3d^9\)) is blue.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct pairings are (1)-(C), (2)-(D), (3)-(A), (4)-(B).

questiontext.text:
Match the \(3d\) metal ions in List I with their calculated spin-only magnetic moments in List II:

List I (Ion)List II (Calculated \(\mu / \mathrm{BM}\))
(1) \(\mathrm{Ti}^{3+}\)(A) \(5.92\)
(2) \(\mathrm{V}^{2+}\)(B) \(3.87\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}\)(C) \(1.73\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\)(D) \(4.90\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For first-row transition metal ions, the spin-only magnetic moment is given by \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mathrm{BM}\), where \(n\) is the number of unpaired \(d\) electrons.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\mathrm{Ti}^{3+}\) (\(Z=22\)) has \(3d^1\) configuration (\(n=1\)): \(\mu = \sqrt{1(3)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\,\mathrm{BM}\).
2. \(\mathrm{V}^{2+}\) (\(Z=23\)) has \(3d^3\) configuration (\(n=3\)): \(\mu = \sqrt{3(5)} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\,\mathrm{BM}\).
3. \(\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}\) (\(Z=24\)) has \(3d^4\) configuration (\(n=4\)): \(\mu = \sqrt{4(6)} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\,\mathrm{BM}\).
4. \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) (\(Z=25\)) has \(3d^5\) configuration (\(n=5\)): \(\mu = \sqrt{5(7)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\,\mathrm{BM}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(C), (2)-(B), (3)-(D), (4)-(A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q05 - Outer electronic configurations of 4d and 5d metals

questiontext.text:
Match the \(4d\) and \(5d\) transition elements in List I with their ground-state outer electronic configurations in List II:

List I (Element)List II (Outer Configuration)
(1) \(\mathrm{Nb}\) (\(Z=41\))(A) \(4d^{10}5s^0\)
(2) \(\mathrm{Pd}\) (\(Z=46\))(B) \(5d^{10}6s^1\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Pt}\) (\(Z=78\))(C) \(4d^4 5s^1\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Au}\) (\(Z=79\))(D) \(5d^9 6s^1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because the energy difference between \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) orbitals is very small, several \(4d\) and \(5d\) transition metals exhibit exceptions to the simple \((n-1)d^x ns^2\) filling order.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Niobium (\(\mathrm{Nb}, Z=41\)) has the outer configuration \(4d^4 5s^1\). Palladium (\(\mathrm{Pd}, Z=46\)) is the only \(d\)-block element with zero electrons in its outermost \(s\) orbital, having configuration \(4d^{10}5s^0\). Platinum (\(\mathrm{Pt}, Z=78\)) has \(5d^9 6s^1\), while gold (\(\mathrm{Au}, Z=79\)) has \(5d^{10}6s^1\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matches are (1)-(C), (2)-(A), (3)-(D), (4)-(B).

questiontext.text:
Match the \(3d\)-metal oxides/oxocations in List I with their characteristic nature in List II:

List I (Species)List II (Nature / Property)
(1) \(\mathrm{CrO}\)(A) Covalent acidic green oil
(2) \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)(B) Basic oxide
(3) \(\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7\)(C) Oxocation stabilising \(\mathrm{V}^{\mathrm{V}}\)
(4) \(\mathrm{VO}_2^+\)(D) Amphoteric oxide

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As the oxidation state of a transition metal in its oxide increases, the ionic character decreases and the acidic character increases.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Chromium(II) oxide (\(\mathrm{CrO}\)) is a low-oxidation-state oxide and is basic. Chromium(III) oxide (\(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) is amphoteric. Manganese(VII) oxide (\(\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7\)) is a covalent green oil that dissolves in water to give permanganic acid (\(\mathrm{HMnO}_4\)), so it is acidic. Vanadium(V) is stabilised in aqueous solution as the oxocation \(\mathrm{VO}_2^+\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are (1)-(B), (2)-(D), (3)-(A), (4)-(C).

questiontext.text:
Match the materials in List I with their compositions or descriptions in List II:

List I (Material)List II (Composition / Description)
(1) Brass(A) \(\sim 95\%\) lanthanoid metal and \(\sim 5\%\) iron
(2) Bronze(B) Non-stoichiometric interstitial compound
(3) Mischmetall(C) Alloy of copper and zinc
(4) \(\mathrm{VH}_{0.56}\)(D) Alloy of copper and tin

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition metals readily form alloys with metals of comparable atomic radii (within about \(15\%\)) and form interstitial compounds when small atoms like \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{C}\), or \(\mathrm{N}\) occupy interstices of the metal lattice.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Brass is a copper–zinc alloy, whereas bronze is a copper–tin alloy. Mischmetall is a well-known alloy consisting of a lanthanoid metal (\(\sim 95\%\)) and iron (\(\sim 5\%\)) with traces of \(\mathrm{S, C, Ca, Al}\). \(\mathrm{VH}_{0.56}\) is a non-stoichiometric interstitial hydride formed by trapping hydrogen atoms inside the vanadium crystal lattice.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(C), (2)-(D), (3)-(A), (4)-(B).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q08 - Trends in M3+ to M2+ standard electrode potentials

questiontext.text:
Match the \(\mathrm{M}^{3+}/\mathrm{M}^{2+}\) redox couples in List I with the electronic basis of their standard electrode potential trends in List II:

List I (Redox Couple)List II (Reason for \(E^\circ\) Value)
(1) \(\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}/\mathrm{Sc}^{2+}\)(A) Comparatively low value due to extra stability of \(d^5\) \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)
(2) \(\mathrm{V}^{3+}/\mathrm{V}^{2+}\)(B) Very low value due to noble gas configuration of \(\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}/\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\)(C) Comparatively low value due to stability of half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level in \(\mathrm{V}^{2+}\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\)(D) High positive value due to extra stability of \(d^5\) \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M}^{3+}/\mathrm{M}^{2+})\) value reflects the relative stability of the \(+3\) and \(+2\) oxidation states in aqueous solution.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
\(\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}\) attains the noble gas \([\mathrm{Ar}]\) configuration, giving a very low \(E^\circ\) value. \(\mathrm{V}^{2+}\) (\(d^3\)) has a stable half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level, resulting in a negative \(E^\circ(\mathrm{V}^{3+}/\mathrm{V}^{2+}) = -0.26\,\mathrm{V}\). \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) has a particularly stable half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration, making reduction of \(\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}\) to \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) strongly favourable (\(E^\circ = +1.57\,\mathrm{V}\)). For iron, \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) has the stable \(3d^5\) configuration, so \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77\,\mathrm{V}\) is comparatively lower than that of manganese.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matches are (1)-(B), (2)-(C), (3)-(D), (4)-(A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q09 - Oxidising action of acidified potassium dichromate

questiontext.text:
Match the reducing species in List I with the products formed when they are oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate (\(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7\)) in List II:

List I (Reducing Species)List II (Oxidation Product)
(1) \(\mathrm{I}^-\)(A) \(\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}\)
(2) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)(B) \(\mathrm{I}_2\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}\)(C) \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\)(D) \(\mathrm{S}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In acidic solution, dichromate acts as a strong oxidising agent via \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-} + 14\mathrm{H}^+ + 6\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} + 7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (\(E^\circ = 1.33\,\mathrm{V}\)).

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Acidified \(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7\) oxidises iodides (\(\mathrm{I}^-\)) to iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_2\)), hydrogen sulphide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)) to elemental sulphur (\(\mathrm{S}\)), tin(II) (\(\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}\)) to tin(IV) (\(\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}\)), and iron(II) (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\)) to iron(III) (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(B), (2)-(D), (3)-(A), (4)-(C).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q10 - Permanganate oxidations in acidic and alkaline media

questiontext.text:
Match the reactions of \(\mathrm{KMnO}_4\) in List I with the corresponding oxidation products in List II:

List I (Reductant and Medium)List II (Product)
(1) \(\mathrm{I}^-\) in acidic medium(A) \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)
(2) \(\mathrm{I}^-\) in neutral or faintly alkaline medium(B) \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\)
(3) \(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{O}_4^{2-}\) in acidic medium(C) \(\mathrm{IO}_3^-\)
(4) \(\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3^{2-}\) in neutral or faintly alkaline medium(D) \(\mathrm{I}_2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The oxidising behaviour and products of potassium permanganate depend on the \(\mathrm{pH}\) of the reaction medium.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
1. In acidic solution, iodide is oxidised to free iodine: \(10\mathrm{I}^- + 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 16\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 5\mathrm{I}_2\).
2. In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, iodide is oxidised to iodate: \(2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{I}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{OH}^- + \mathrm{IO}_3^-\).
3. In acidic solution at \(333\,\mathrm{K}\), oxalate is oxidised to \(\mathrm{CO}_2\): \(5\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{O}_4^{2-} + 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 16\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 10\mathrm{CO}_2\).
4. In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, thiosulphate is oxidised to sulphate: \(8\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 3\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3^{2-} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 8\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 6\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-} + 2\mathrm{OH}^-\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(D), (2)-(C), (3)-(A), (4)-(B).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q11 - Electronic configurations of trivalent lanthanoid ions

questiontext.text:
Match the trivalent lanthanoid ions in List I with their outer \(4f\) electronic configurations (outside the \([\mathrm{Xe}]\) core) in List II:

List I (Ion)List II (Configuration)
(1) \(\mathrm{La}^{3+}\) (\(Z=57\))(A) \(4f^7\)
(2) \(\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}\) (\(Z=58\))(B) \(4f^{14}\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Gd}^{3+}\) (\(Z=64\))(C) \(4f^0\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Lu}^{3+}\) (\(Z=71\))(D) \(4f^1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All tripositive lanthanoid ions (\(\mathrm{Ln}^{3+}\)) have electronic configurations of the form \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^n\), where \(n\) increases from \(0\) to \(14\) across \(\mathrm{La}^{3+}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu}^{3+}\).

Step 2: Individual Pairings
1. \(\mathrm{La}\) (\(5d^1 6s^2\)) loses three electrons to give \(\mathrm{La}^{3+}\): \(4f^0\).
2. \(\mathrm{Ce}\) (\(4f^1 5d^1 6s^2\)) loses three electrons to give \(\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}\): \(4f^1\).
3. \(\mathrm{Gd}\) (\(4f^7 5d^1 6s^2\)) loses three electrons to give \(\mathrm{Gd}^{3+}\): \(4f^7\).
4. \(\mathrm{Lu}\) (\(4f^{14} 5d^1 6s^2\)) loses three electrons to give \(\mathrm{Lu}^{3+}\): \(4f^{14}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(C), (2)-(D), (3)-(A), (4)-(B).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q12 - Lanthanoid ions with +2 and +4 oxidation states

questiontext.text:
Match the lanthanoid ions in List I with their electronic configurations and redox properties in List II:

List I (Ion)List II (Configuration & Property)
(1) \(\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}\)(A) \(4f^{14}\) configuration; \(+2\) reductant
(2) \(\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}\)(B) \(4f^7\) configuration; \(+4\) oxidant
(3) \(\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}\)(C) \(4f^7\) configuration; strong \(+2\) reducing agent
(4) \(\mathrm{Tb}^{4+}\)(D) \(4f^0\) noble-gas configuration; analytical oxidant

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While \(+3\) is the predominant oxidation state of lanthanoids, \(+2\) and \(+4\) ions occur when they achieve extra stability from empty (\(4f^0\)), half-filled (\(4f^7\)), or completely filled (\(4f^{14}\)) \(f\) subshells.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
\(\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}\) has the \(4f^0\) noble-gas configuration and acts as a strong oxidant (\(E^\circ = +1.74\,\mathrm{V}\)) used as an analytical reagent. \(\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}\) has the \(4f^7\) configuration and is a strong reducing agent reverting to \(+3\). \(\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}\) has the \(4f^{14}\) configuration and is a reductant. \(\mathrm{Tb}^{4+}\) has half-filled \(4f^7\) orbitals and acts as an oxidant.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct pairings are (1)-(D), (2)-(C), (3)-(A), (4)-(B).

questiontext.text:
Match the actinoid elements in List I with their ground-state outer electronic configurations (outside the \([\mathrm{Rn}]\) core) in List II:

List I (Element)List II (Outer Configuration)
(1) \(\mathrm{Th}\) (\(Z=90\))(A) \(5f^7 6d^1 7s^2\)
(2) \(\mathrm{U}\) (\(Z=92\))(B) \(6d^2 7s^2\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Am}\) (\(Z=95\))(C) \(5f^3 6d^1 7s^2\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Cm}\) (\(Z=96\))(D) \(5f^7 7s^2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Actinoids have \(7s^2\) in common with variable occupancy of the \(5f\) and \(6d\) subshells due to comparable energies and the stability of \(5f^0\), \(5f^7\), and \(5f^{14}\) occupancies.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Thorium (\(\mathrm{Th}, Z=90\)) has no \(5f\) electrons in its ground state: \(6d^2 7s^2\). Uranium (\(\mathrm{U}, Z=92\)) has \(5f^3 6d^1 7s^2\). Americium (\(\mathrm{Am}, Z=95\)) achieves a half-filled \(5f^7\) subshell with configuration \(5f^7 7s^2\). Curium (\(\mathrm{Cm}, Z=96\)) retains the stable half-filled \(5f^7\) subshell by placing the next electron in \(6d\), giving \(5f^7 6d^1 7s^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(B), (2)-(C), (3)-(D), (4)-(A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_Q14 - Maximum oxidation states of early actinoids

questiontext.text:
Match the early actinoid elements in List I with their maximum known oxidation states in List II:

List I (Actinoid)List II (Maximum Oxidation State)
(1) \(\mathrm{Th}\)(A) \(+6\)
(2) \(\mathrm{Pa}\)(B) \(+4\)
(3) \(\mathrm{U}\)(C) \(+7\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Np}\)(D) \(+5\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because the \(5f\), \(6d\), and \(7s\) levels have comparable energies, early actinoids exhibit a wide range of oxidation states, with the maximum oxidation state increasing regularly from \(\mathrm{Th}\) to \(\mathrm{Np}\).

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Thorium (\(\mathrm{Th}\)) shows a maximum oxidation state of \(+4\); Protactinium (\(\mathrm{Pa}\)) shows \(+5\); Uranium (\(\mathrm{U}\)) shows \(+6\); and Neptunium (\(\mathrm{Np}\)) reaches \(+7\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(B), (2)-(D), (3)-(A), (4)-(C).

questiontext.text:
Match the \(3d\) transition metals in List I with the formulas of their highest-oxidation-state simple halides in List II:

List I (Metal)List II (Highest Simple Halide)
(1) \(\mathrm{Ti}\)(A) \(\mathrm{VF}_5\)
(2) \(\mathrm{V}\)(B) \(\mathrm{MnF}_4\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Cr}\)(C) \(\mathrm{TiX}_4\) (\(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{F} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}\))
(4) \(\mathrm{Mn}\)(D) \(\mathrm{CrF}_6\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fluorine stabilises the highest oxidation states in simple halides of \(3d\) metals due to high lattice energy or high covalent bond enthalpy.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
Titanium forms all tetrahalides \(\mathrm{TiX}_4\) (\(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{F}, \mathrm{Cl}, \mathrm{Br}, \mathrm{I}\)). Vanadium achieves \(+5\) only in \(\mathrm{VF}_5\). Chromium achieves \(+6\) in \(\mathrm{CrF}_6\). Manganese does not form a simple heptahalide; its highest simple halide is \(\mathrm{MnF}_4\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(C), (2)-(A), (3)-(D), (4)-(B).

questiontext.text:
Match the reactions involving manganate and permanganate species in List I with their products in List II:

List I (Reaction)List II (Products)
(1) Thermal decomposition of \(\mathrm{KMnO}_4\) at \(513\,\mathrm{K}\)(A) \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-} + \mathrm{H}^+\)
(2) Disproportionation of \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-}\) in acidic solution(B) \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + \mathrm{NO}_3^- + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
(3) Oxidation of \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) by \(\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8^{2-}\) in water(C) \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + \mathrm{MnO}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
(4) Oxidation of \(\mathrm{NO}_2^-\) by \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) in acidic solution(D) \(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{MnO}_4 + \mathrm{MnO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Manganese compounds undergo characteristic thermal decomposition, disproportionation, and redox reactions depending on the oxidising agent and acidity of the medium.

Step 2: Individual Pairings
1. Heating \(\mathrm{KMnO}_4\) at \(513\,\mathrm{K}\) yields \(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{MnO}_4\), \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\), and \(\mathrm{O}_2\): \(2\mathrm{KMnO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{MnO}_4 + \mathrm{MnO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\).
2. In acidic solution, \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-}\) disproportionates: \(3\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-} + 4\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).
3. Peroxodisulphate oxidises \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) to permanganate in the laboratory: \(2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 5\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8^{2-} + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 10\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-} + 16\mathrm{H}^+\).
4. Acidified \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) oxidises nitrite to nitrate: \(5\mathrm{NO}_2^- + 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 6\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 5\mathrm{NO}_3^- + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are (1)-(D), (2)-(C), (3)-(A), (4)-(B).
